raw.caption: Thinking about getting a Staffy? 🐶 Think again… The Staffordshire Bull Terrier was built in the Black Country and the backstreets of Birmingham in the early 1800s, when breeders crossed the old bulldog with local terriers to create the bull-and-terrier. The aim was a dog with the bulldog's strength and the terrier's speed. Bull-baiting was outlawed by the Cruelty to Animals Act of 1835, but the dogs carried on being used in illegal pits for decades afterwards. Here's the part most people miss: those dogs were handled in the pit by people, so any dog who turned on a human was removed from the bloodline. That's exactly why the breed today is so ridiculously soft with us. The Kennel Club only recognised the breed in May 1935, almost a century after the sport it came from was banned. The Staffordshire Bull Terrier Club formed the same year, and the first breed standard was drawn up at a meeting held in a Black Country pub. The Kennel Club's own standard describes them as bold, fearless and totally reliable, and highly intelligent and affectionate, especially with children. "Totally reliable" is about as strong as it gets in a breed standard. They're often called the nanny dog, though there's no historical evidence for it. The nickname only appears from the 1970s onwards, so it's best taken as affection rather than fact, and supervision around little ones is always sensible whatever the breed. Worth knowing: the Staffy is a legal, Kennel Club recognised British breed. It is not banned, it is not a Pit Bull, and it is not an XL Bully, though it does get mistaken for all three. In 2019 the British public voted the Staffordshire Bull Terrier the nation's favourite dog on ITV. Yet they remain one of the most common breeds sitting in UK rescue centres, waiting for someone to look past the reputation.
